verdict.rationale: Each named activity is lexically attested as a real corporate practice. Neh 8:1 to 8:8 records the public reading of the torah paired with exposition that yields understanding, Acts 2:42 lists apostolic teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread, and the prayers, 1 Tim 4:13 commands anagnosis, paraklesis, and didaskalia, 2 Tim 4:2 commands kerysson ton logon, and Col 3:16 with 1 Cor 14:26 adds song and psalms as corporate elements. What the words do not establish is the proportional claim carried by centers. Acts 2:42 coordinates four practices in parallel datives joined by kai with no comparative, superlative, or ordinal marker, and Acts 20:7 names klasai arton as the purpose-infinitive of the gathering with Paul's logos following within that purpose. The constituent claim is well attested. The centering claim is underdetermined by the vocabulary.

scripture.force: All the assembled people gather as one and ask Ezra to bring the book of the torah for public reading. The corporate scope, kol haam (all the people) gathered keish echad (as one man), frames Scripture reading as a congregational act rather than a private one.

Ezra reads (qara, wayyiqra in 8:3) from the torah from morning until midday before the men, the women, and all who could understand (mebinim), and the ears of all the people were attentive to the book. Sustained public reading occupies the gathering, and the hearers' attentiveness is highlighted.

They read in the book, in the torah of God, meporash (a Pual participle of parash, made distinct or clear), and giving the sense (sekel), so that the people understood (bin) the reading. Reading is paired with explanation that yields comprehension, the lexical core of preaching as exposition.

Ezra blesses Yahweh, and the people answer Amen, Amen, lifting their hands and bowing in worship. Prayer and bodily worship accompany the reading, showing multiple practices interwoven within one gathering rather than reading alone.

Until I come, devote yourself (prosece, present active imperative) to the public reading (te anagnosei), to exhortation (te paraklesei), to teaching (te didaskalia). Three datives joined by repeated articles mark three standing components of the gathered ministry as co-objects of one imperative. Reading, exhortation, and teaching share one verbal command.

Preach (keryxon, aorist imperative) the word (ton logon), be ready in season and out of season, reprove (elegxon), rebuke (epitimeson), exhort (parakaleson) with all patience and teaching (didache). The proclamation of the word is commanded as a defining ministerial act paired with teaching, but as a charge to Timothy as evangelist, not a script for the relative weight of elements in the corporate gathering.

They were devoting themselves (esan proskarterountes, periphrastic imperfect) to the apostles' teaching (te didache), and the fellowship (te koinonia), the breaking of bread (te klasei tou artou), and the prayers (tais proseuchais). Four datives, each governed by its own article (te, te, te, tais), are joined to one participle by two kai coordinators with no comparative or superlative marker. Lexically the four stand in parallel, which complicates a claim that any one is the structural center.

On the first of the week, when we were gathered (synegmenon hemon, genitive absolute) to break bread (klasai arton, aorist infinitive of purpose), Paul was discoursing with them (dielegeto) and prolonged the word (parateinen ton logon) until midnight. The infinitive klasai arton names the purpose of the gathering, with Paul's logos occurring within that purpose rather than being named as the center.

Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly (ho logos tou Christou enoikeito en hymin plousios), teaching and admonishing one another in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs (psalmois, hymnois, odais pneumatikais), singing (adontes) with grace in your hearts to God. The verse pairs word-rich indwelling with mutual teaching expressed through song, lexically binding word and song together rather than ranking one over the other.

When you come together (hotan synerchesthe), each one has a psalm (psalmon), a teaching (didachen), a revelation, a tongue, an interpretation; let all things be done for edification (pros oikodomen). Five elements are coordinated as items each member brings to the gathering, with edification as the goal. The vocabulary names goal but not a single centering element.

complicating_texts.resolution: The verse lists four practices in coordinated datives, each carrying its own article (te didache, te koinonia, te klasei tou artou, tais proseuchais), joined to a single periphrastic participle proskarterountes by two kai coordinators. There is no comparative, superlative, or ordinal marker ranking teaching above the others. Lexically the four stand in parallel, so the text supports their joint presence but does not by itself establish that reading and preaching center the gathering. This bounds the verdict to disputed rather than a clean affirmation of the centering claim.

Five activities are coordinated as items each member brings to the gathering (psalmon, didachen, apokalypsin, glossan, hermeneian), and the controlling clause panta pros oikodomen ginestho names edification as the goal of all of them. The lexemes set teaching alongside song, revelation, tongue, and interpretation without ranking, and they fix the criterion as oikodome rather than as a single centering element. The vocabulary therefore underdetermines a centering claim while affirming the breadth of constituent elements.

The genitive absolute synegmenon hemon klasai arton makes klasai arton the stated purpose-infinitive of the gathering on the first day of the week, with Paul's dielegeto and parateinen ton logon occurring within that purpose. The lexical pressure runs against the proposition that the sermon names the center of the gathering, while still affirming that proclamation occupies its proceedings.

variants.note: Bundle reports not_in_ecm_scope true and supplies no variant units. The Acts 2:42 reading carries a diacritic at koinonia in the SBLGNT apparatus reflecting punctuation variation between te koinonia te klasei and te koinonia, te klasei, but neither punctuation alters the presence and parallelism of the four datives, and no cited verse turns on a contested reading for this verdict.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Reading each anchor as listing constituent worship activities, the lexemes for reading (anagnosis, qara), exposition (parash, sekel, bin), teaching (didache, didaskalia), proclamation (kerysso), prayer (proseuche), breaking of bread (klasis tou artou, klasai arton), and song (psalmos, ode, ado) are all present across both testaments. The constituent claim is well attested.

Reading the claim as asserting that reading and preaching hold structural primacy over the other elements, the lexemes provide no comparative or superlative marker ranking them above prayer, song, or the Supper. Acts 2:42 coordinates four practices without hierarchy, 1 Cor 14:26 coordinates five with oikodome as goal, and Acts 20:7 names klasai arton as the purpose-infinitive of the gathering. A primacy claim is not lexically fixed.

Reading the claim through the criterion panta pros oikodomen ginestho of 1 Cor 14:26, the words name edification as the controlling goal of every gathered element rather than naming a single centering act. On this lens the proposition is neither affirmed nor denied, since centering and edification are different lexical claims.

hermeneutics.notes: The verdict hinges on which reading of the stem is in view. Constituent presence is affirmable across both testaments. Proportional centering is not. That divergence yields a disputed result on the stem as worded.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: Christian worship in the cited texts includes the public reading and exposition of Scripture together with prayer, the breaking of bread, song, and other corporate acts. The lexical pattern attests these as constituent practices without fixing their relative proportion.
stem_audit.notes: The phrase rightly centers on embeds two layered verdicts in the stem, a normative judgment carried by rightly and a proportional ranking carried by centers. The lexical store can attest the presence of each named element but cannot by itself establish a hierarchy or proportion among them, and it cannot adjudicate the normative rightly. The verdict is derived on the original stem and lands at disputed because the constituent claim is supportable while the centering claim is not lexically demonstrable.

lay_summary: The texts behind this question all show worship made up of several activities done together. In Nehemiah 8 Ezra brings out the book of the law and reads it aloud to the whole assembly from morning until midday, while Levites give the sense so the people understand what is read. Reading and explaining sit side by side. The two letters to Timothy command devotion to the public reading, to exhortation, and to teaching, and they command preaching the word in season and out of season with patience and instruction. So the words clearly attest public reading and preaching as real parts of the gathering. The harder part of the question is the word centers. The claim says worship rightly centers on reading and preaching, with the other practices alongside. Here the words give less help, and it is worth being precise about why. In Acts 2:42 four practices are listed, each with its own little word for the, joined only by and, with no marker that ranks teaching above the prayers or the breaking of bread. The text presents them in a row, not a stack. In Acts 20:7 the disciples gather to break bread, which is the stated reason for the meeting, and Paul's long talk happens within that gathering rather than being named as its center. In 1 Corinthians 14:26 each member brings a psalm, a teaching, a revelation, a tongue, or an interpretation, and the rule given is that all things be done for building up, naming a goal rather than a single centering act. In Colossians 3:16 the word of Christ dwelling richly and teaching one another in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs are bound together in one sentence. So the words clearly support that reading, preaching, prayer, the breaking of bread, and song are all genuine parts of Christian worship. But the words do not by themselves rank these elements or say that one of them holds first place. For that reason the result here is disputed, strong on the presence of each element but unable to fix their relative weight from the language alone.
